sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** The purple "Keep your streak going" box (about x 56–456, y 390–498) sits right under the only call to action. It speaks to people who already use the app ("keep your streak going"), but this page is for people who have not signed up. To a first-time visitor it says nothing about why to start. It is also a saturated, filled, rounded block larger than the orange button, so it looks like a second button and pulls the eye away from "Start your free week". The fact it states (five days in a row means twice as likely to finish) could help as proof. As a box shouting at newcomers about a streak they don't have, it competes with the main task, which is getting the visitor to start (Nielsen, *10 Usability Heuristics*, no. 8: aesthetic and minimalist design). Fix: remove it, or turn the fact into a quiet line of plain text that backs the "ten weeks" promise, so the button is the only filled block in the left column. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** The teal panel (about x 676–1076, y 110–410) holds two empty speech bubbles. That is the word "conversation" drawn as a stock icon. It adds nothing the headline hasn't already said: no language, no tutor, no sign of the speaking-first method or of being able to talk after ten weeks. It is the biggest shape on the page and it tells the viewer the least. It is also what makes the page look like a template. Fix: use the space to show what is different here, such as a real exchange in Spanish or French with the tutor's feedback on each word, or a lesson screen. Then the picture proves the headline instead of repeating it. Taste (the catalog entry has no approved source; argued on its own terms). Weight: major.
3. **Apart from the pictures, do the type, colors, and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** Three unrelated saturated hues sit in one hero: burnt orange (button), violet (streak box) and teal (image panel). They share no temperature or value and are not used anywhere else on the page. The rest of the page is neutral grey and black. So the hero reads as three separately chosen blocks, not one palette, and no colour signals "this is the action". Fix: keep one accent for action (the orange) and one supporting brand colour at most. Bring the others into that family or make them neutral. Taste (no approved source in the catalog entry; common sense about unity). Weight: minor on its own; it mostly goes away if finding 1 is fixed.

**What's working.** The headline makes a specific, checkable promise ("Hold a real conversation in ten weeks"). The subhead says exactly what you get: short daily lessons that start with speaking, four named languages, and a tutor that listens. A first-time viewer can say what this is in one sentence. The three numbered steps (Listen, Speak, Use it) have headings that name what each step holds, and each has a one-line description in plain words.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 5 yes, 3 no (image and headline make one idea; every element does a job; one mood, not a collage)

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** No. The headline (about x 56–600, y 110–205) leads on size, but three saturated blocks compete with it on contrast and with each other: the teal illustration panel (x 676–1076, y 110–410), the orange "Start your free week" button (x 56–303, y 303–361), and the purple "Keep your streak going" card (x 56–456, y 390–498). The viewer reads the headline, then looks across to the teal panel, which is the largest block of colour on the page and shows nothing but two generic speech bubbles. Then the eye drops to a tie: the purple card is larger than the button, just as saturated, and sits 28 px below it, so it looks like a second call to action. The one thing the page wants the viewer to do loses its pull to a retention tip that means nothing to someone who hasn't signed up yet. When three or more elements have the same strength of colour and none is clearly stronger, the order of importance is gone (Tschichold, *The New Typography*; Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*). Fix: keep the headline first, then make the orange button clearly the second thing seen and set the rest back. Calm the purple card down to a neutral tint or plain text, or move it out of the hero, since a streak message fits a later stage of the user journey. Tone down the teal panel by making it lighter or smaller, or by letting a real product image carry it, so its colour mass doesn't outweigh the headline and the button. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.**
- The headline is far larger and heavier than everything else, about 44 px bold against roughly 18 px for the lede, so the start of the text is clear even though the colour blocks fight it.
- The step headings ("1. Listen", "2. Speak", "3. Use it") are bold and dark over regular grey body text. Weight and colour do the separating, not just a near-identical size, so the levels read at a glance even at about 17 px against 15 px.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (one element dominates)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do all blocks, pictures included, take their edges and the gaps between them from one grid, so column lines and gutters repeat down the page?** Also **Do the main divisions of the frame follow one proportion?** Both answer no. The steps row below the hero sets a clean three-column grid: 56–413, 461–819 and 867–1224, with even 48 px gutters. The hero ignores it. The text column wraps at about 615 px, and the teal picture runs from 676 to 1076 px. That left edge matches no column line and the page center is 640, so the split is neither halves nor thirds. The right edge stops 148 px short of the 1224 margin that the nav and steps both reach.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the hero image looks placed by eye. The empty strip on its right reads as unfinished space rather than chosen space, and the top half and bottom half of the page don't look like one system.
   - **Why:** Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid" and "The photograph in the grid system".
   - **Fix:** take the hero split from the same columns as the steps row. For example, put text over the first column and a half, and run the picture from 461 or 867 out to the 1224 margin. Also line the picture's top and bottom up with the headline's first line and the last element of the text column.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, major.
2. **Is the space inside each group clearly smaller than the space between groups, so each heading sits nearer the text it introduces?** No. The purple "Keep your streak going" card sits 28 px below the "Start your free week" button. That's the same gap as subhead to button (about 30 px), so spacing puts it inside the signup group. It's actually a separate message about keeping your streak, aimed at learners who already practice. Meanwhile the gap from the hero to the steps row (card bottom at 498, rule at 551, about 52 px) is the only large break on the page, and it's still small for a change of section.
   - **What the viewer sees:** the streak message gets read as part of the offer, right where the visitor should be deciding to click.
   - **Why:** Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. II, on grouping by proximity.
   - **Fix:** separate the card from the signup group with clearly more space than the gaps inside the group, or move it out of the hero entirely. The "streak" message belongs to existing learners, not a first-visit hero. Open up the hero-to-steps gap so the section change reads.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major.
3. **Do only related elements look alike, with no accidental groups or shapes formed between unrelated ones?** No. The orange button (56–303 × 303–361) and the purple card (56–456 × 390–498) are both saturated, filled, rounded rectangles, stacked flush left on the same edge.
   - **What the viewer sees:** two buttons, or a main and a second choice. The purple card is the bigger and more strongly colored of the two, so it pulls attention from the real call to action. It's also exactly as wide as the teal panel (400 px) and just as saturated, so the two colored blocks start to read as a pair that has nothing to do with the content.
   - **Why:** Gestalt grouping by similarity (`art-direction.md`, "Gestalt grouping: similarity, continuity, closure"; entry not opened).
   - **Fix:** make the button the only filled, saturated shape in the signup area. Recast the streak message as quiet text, or a pale tint or outline that can't be mistaken for a control.
   - **Kind and weight:** defect, major.
4. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. The empty space comes from leftovers, not from a plan:
   - a 148 px strip right of the teal panel (1076–1224, 110–410)
   - an L-shaped pocket under the panel and right of the purple card (456–1224, 410–550)
   - a 180 px empty band under the steps (620–800)

   The bottom band may just be where the screenshot cuts off, but the first two are side effects of the panel being off-grid.
   - **What the viewer sees:** no single open area that reads as chosen, so the right half feels unanchored.
   - **Why:** Ruder, *Typography: A Manual of Design*, "Contrasts" and "Form and counter-form".
   - **Fix:** mostly solved by finding 1. Once the picture reaches the margin, the leftover strips merge into one deliberate open area.
   - **Kind and weight:** convention, minor.

**What's working.**
- Everything on the left (logo, headline, subhead, button, card, first step) hangs from one flush-left edge at 56 px, matching the nav. That gives the left half a strong, readable spine.
- The steps row is the page's best-built part. It has three equal columns with even gutters, a thin rule over each heading, and titles on one shared baseline at about y579. Each heading sits tight to its line of text, so each step reads as one unit and the three read as a sequence.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 8 yes, 5 no (one grid; space shows the groups; no accidental groups; white space gathered; one proportion), 0 unsure

sections.report:
I've finished the Text section walk and the deep read, so here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Text on a plain background reaches 4.5:1 contrast (3:1 for large text): no.** This is the white bold label "Start your free week" on the orange button at about x 56–303, y 303–362. I estimated the orange at roughly #DC4A10 by eye, which puts white on it at about 4.2:1. That passes for large text but not for normal text, and the label looks about 18 px bold. WCAG counts bold text as large only from 18.66 px up, so this label probably has to meet 4.5:1 and narrowly misses (WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.3). Readers with low vision, or anyone on a washed-out screen, get a slightly soft label on the one button that matters most. To check, measure the button colour and the label's font size. To fix, darken the orange a step so it reaches 4.5:1 (it still reads as orange), or set the label at 19 px bold or larger. Marked as a convention. Weight: minor, because the label is still easy to read here and only a narrow margin is at stake.
2. **Headings break at phrase boundaries: no.** The headline at about x 56–600, y 112–205 breaks as "Hold a real conversation in / ten weeks". The "in" belongs to "in ten weeks", so line 1 trails off on a preposition, and the promise ("ten weeks") loses its lead-in and sits alone. Break it as "Hold a real conversation / in ten weeks", using a non-breaking space or a narrower heading box. Then line 1 is the outcome and line 2 is the timeframe, and each reads as one idea. Marked as taste or common sense: the catalog's source for breaks in headings is unverified. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The lede at about y 225–275 runs roughly 63 characters a line with comfortable leading, in grey that still reads clearly on white. It reads in one easy pass.
- The page uses one sans family across the headline, lede, button, purple callout and step labels. Weight and size set the levels with no faces competing. The heading is set tight enough that its two lines read as one unit.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (text on a plain background reaches 4.5:1 contrast; headings break at phrase boundaries)

I've read the colour entries and I'm writing up the report.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the piece use a small palette, about one neutral range and one or two hues besides the status colors?** and **Is strong, saturated color kept to a small share of the area, with most of the area neutral or muted?** (one problem, so one finding):
   - **Where:** Around the neutral greys there are three hues, all saturated and at about the same strength, each on a large element in the hero:
     - an orange-red CTA, "Start your free week" (about x 56–303, y 303–362);
     - a violet "Keep your streak going" card right under it (about x 56–456, y 390–499);
     - a teal illustration panel (about x 676–1076, y 110–410).
   - **What the viewer experiences:** Together they cover only about a sixth of the screen, so the total amount of colour is fine. The problem is that no hue leads. The eye goes from the headline to the orange button, then gets pulled down to the violet card and across to the teal block. The violet card is bigger than the button, sits directly below it, and is drawn as a solid filled block in the same style. So a non-interactive tip competes with the one action the page wants, and on a phone it could pass for a second button. In grayscale the violet is the darkest of the three, so by lightness it outranks the CTA. Three unrelated brand-strength hues on one screen also suggest no colour system: each element got its own colour.
   - **Why:** Itten, *The Art of Color*, on colour chords: keep one hue dominant and mute the others in saturation or area; three equally saturated hues at equal weight is a defect. Refactoring UI, "Define your shades", calls for one neutral ramp and one or two brand hues. Apple HIG, "Color", says to reserve the accent for the main action.
   - **Direction of the fix:**
     - Let the orange CTA be the one lead colour.
     - Make the streak card a light tint, for example a pale violet or pale warm neutral with dark text, or a neutral card with a small coloured icon, so it reads as information rather than a second button.
     - Either bring the teal panel into the same family as the lead colour, or soften it to a light tint or dark shade so it frames the illustration without matching the button's strength.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect. Major.

**What's working.**
- **Warm colour where action is, cool colour where it isn't.** The only warm colour sits on the CTA, and the cool teal sits on the decorative illustration. That puts colour temperature behind the page's one action (Itten, warm-cool contrast). Keep this split when cutting the palette back.
- **Colour has to stand out against a neutral page.** The rest of the page is white with near-black and grey text, and the step cards use thin grey rules instead of fills. That leaves only the accents to carry colour, which is why it matters that only one of them should.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 7 yes, 2 no (small palette; strong colour kept to a small share).

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye goes to the headline, then the orange button, then the purple card. The teal panel on the right is a large, quiet block of colour holding a small line drawing of two speech bubbles. It reads as a consumer language-learning landing page. I'm assuming its job is to get adult learners to start the free week.

Pictures (one illustration, plus the "Parlo" wordmark):
- Every image shows its content: yes
- Full quality, sharp, unstretched: yes (crop 676,110,400,300 is crisp)
- Crops look intended: yes (the bubble group is centred in the panel, about x 760–993 and y 178–352)
- Subject stands apart from background: yes (white strokes on teal)
- One rendering style and level of detail: yes (there is only one illustration)
- Photos share one treatment: yes (there are no photos)
- One stroke weight, cap style and corner radius: yes (the outlines and text-lines look the same weight, with matching rounded corners and tails)
- One viewpoint and light direction: yes (flat drawing)
- Texture or pattern stays quiet: yes (none)
- No fake bevels, textures or depth: yes (flat)
- Logo has clear space, no distortion, own colours: yes ("Parlo" at 56,30 has plenty of room)
- Logo simple enough to read small and in one colour: yes (plain bold wordmark)

No line was answered no or unsure, so step 5 is not needed.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies. There is one line illustration in the hero (teal panel, x 676–1076, y 110–410) and the "Parlo" wordmark.

**Findings**
None.

One point for the director that no checklist line covers. The illustration is two generic speech bubbles with placeholder lines. They say "chat" but nothing about speaking aloud, a tutor that listens, or the four languages. Any messaging, support or social product could use the same picture, so the largest image on the page adds nothing beyond the headline. It also puts a small drawing (about 235×175 px) inside a 400×300 panel, so the panel reads mostly as an empty block of colour. Fix: show what is actually different here, such as speaking and getting feedback on each word, or a glimpse of a real lesson, or make the drawing fill more of the panel. Taste, but it costs the hero its chance to show the product. Weight: minor to major, depending on how much the director leans on the hero.

**What's working.** The illustration is drawn cleanly: one white stroke weight, consistent rounded corners and matching tails, so it looks deliberate rather than pieced together from different sets. The "Parlo" wordmark is plain text with plenty of space around it, so it stays readable at nav size and in any single colour.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Charts and data: skipped. The page has no chart, table of figures or dashboard. It is a landing page with a header, a hero, an illustration and three numbered steps.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Charts and data: skipped

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a primary button, a nav bar and a Log in link.

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower? / Does every control look like what it does?**
   - **Where:** The purple "Keep your streak going" block at about (56,390)–(456,498) sits 30 px under the orange "Start your free week" button at (56,303)–(303,361).
   - **Problem:** It has the same treatment as the button: a filled, saturated, rounded box with bold white text. It is also larger, wider and sits on its own row.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The eye goes from the headline to the orange button and is pulled straight down to the purple block. It reads as a second pressable action or a clickable card. The visitor has to work out which one is the real action, and may tap the purple block and get nothing if it is only information.
   - **Why:** It breaks Material Design 3, "Buttons": one high-emphasis action per view, and the rest lower. It also gives a false signifier (Norman, *The Design of Everyday Things*, ch. 1): it looks pressable but probably isn't.
   - **Fix:** Give the view one high-emphasis action, the orange button. If the streak note is information, take away its button look: no saturated fill, use a quiet tint, a rule or plain text, and move it out of the CTA's column. If it is meant to be clickable, make it a clearly secondary style, such as outlined or a text link.
   - Defect. Weight: major.

2. **Do labels and messages use the audience's own words rather than internal or system terms?**
   - **Where:** The same purple block, heading "Keep your streak going".
   - **Problem:** The page looks logged-out (there's a "Log in" link and a "Start your free week" offer), so most viewers are first-time visitors. They have no streak to keep. The heading speaks to an existing user in the product's own word for daily use, so a stranger is left wondering whether this message is meant for them.
   - **Why:** Nielsen heuristic 2, Match between system and the real world. Applying it here, to a mismatch of user state rather than jargon, is my judgment.
   - **Fix:** Write it for the visitor, and make the payoff about them: for example, that practising five days in a row doubles their chance of finishing. Or show this block only to signed-in users.
   - Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- The "Start your free week" button is the one warm, solid shape on the page. It sits right under the subhead, and its label names exactly what the visitor gets and for how long.
- The header follows the usual pattern: logo at left, plain text nav at right, Log in at the far end. Visitors find their way without thinking.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and focus states on the CTA and the nav links.
- Whether the purple block is actually clickable. If it is, finding 1 changes from a false signifier to two competing primary actions; the fix is the same.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 29 yes, 3 no (one primary action; controls look like what they do; audience's own words), 1 unsure (focus indicator 2 px with 3:1 contrast).
